say: You give it a population mean $\mu$, a standard deviation $\sigma$ and a sample size $n$. It tells you how the mean of a sample, $\bar{x}$, behaves.

The key idea: sample means centre on $\mu$, but they spread out much less than single values. The spread is the **standard error**, $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$. Use it in place of $\sigma$ when you standardise.

how.higher: Higher level only, on Paper 2, as part of the statistics question: find the standard error, then a probability for a sample mean. It is worth 5 to 20 marks.

example.question: The weight of a bag of flour is normally distributed with mean $500$ g and standard deviation $12$ g. A sample of $36$ bags is taken. Find the probability that the mean weight of the sample is greater than $503$ g.

steps.title: Find the standard error
steps.say: The sample mean has the same mean, $500$. Its spread is the standard error: divide $\sigma$ by $\sqrt{n}$.

steps.title: Standardise the sample mean
steps.say: Turn $503$ into a $z$-score. Use the standard error as the spread.

steps.title: Read the tables
steps.say: The tables give the area to the left of $z$. We want the area to the right, so take it from $1$.

say: You give it a sample proportion $\hat{p}$ and the sample size $n$. It gives an interval that the true proportion lies in, with $95\%$ confidence.
The key idea: the standard error of a proportion is $\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})}{n}}$. Go $1.96$ of those either side of $\hat{p}$.

how.higher: Higher level asks for it on Paper 2, as a part of its own in the statistics question, worth 5 to 15 marks. The interval is then often used to test a claim.
how.ordinary: Ordinary level asks for it on Paper 2, usually as a 5 mark part. It uses the shorter version, $\hat{p} \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$, after a part that finds $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$.

example.question: In a random sample of $500$ voters, $120$ say they will vote for a new candidate. Find a $95\%$ confidence interval for the proportion of all voters who will vote for her. Give the limits to $4$ decimal places.

steps.title: Find the sample proportion
steps.say: The sample proportion is the number who said yes, divided by the sample size.

steps.title: Find the margin of error
steps.say: The margin of error is $1.96$ times the standard error. Put $\hl{1}{0.24}$ and $n = 500$ into the formula.

steps.title: Go either side of the proportion
steps.say: Subtract $\hl{2}{E}$ for the lower limit and add it for the upper limit.

lines.text: State it as an interval: $0.2026 \le p \le 0.2774$.

say: You give it a sample mean $\bar{x}$, a standard deviation and a sample size $n$. It gives an interval that the population mean lies in, with $95\%$ confidence.
The key idea: the sample mean is off from $\mu$ by about one standard error, $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$. Go $1.96$ standard errors either side of $\bar{x}$.

say: You give it a claimed mean $\mu_0$ and a sample: $\bar{x}$, $\sigma$ and $n$. It decides whether the sample is far enough from the claim to reject it.
The key idea: the $z$ statistic counts how many standard errors $\bar{x}$ is from $\mu_0$. At the $5\%$ level, beyond $\pm 1.96$ is too far to be chance.

how.higher: Higher level only, on Paper 2, in most years. It is a part of the statistics question worth 10 to 15 marks: state the hypotheses, find $z$, then give a conclusion in context.

example.question: A machine is set to fill bags with a mean of $250$ g. The standard deviation is $6$ g. A sample of $36$ bags has a mean of $247.9$ g. Test, at the $5\%$ level of significance, whether the mean fill has changed. State your hypotheses and your conclusion.

steps.title: State the hypotheses
steps.say: The null hypothesis says nothing has changed. The alternative says the mean is different, in either direction.

lines.text: $H_1$: the mean fill is not $250$ g.

steps.title: Find the z statistic
steps.say: Subtract the claimed mean from $\bar{x}$. Divide by the standard error, $\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$.

steps.title: Compare with the limits
steps.say: At the $5\%$ level, the limits are $-1.96$ and $1.96$. Is $\hl{1}{z}$ outside them?

lines.text: $-2.1$ is less than $-1.96$, so $z$ is in the rejection zone.

steps.title: Write the conclusion
steps.say: Say what it means for the machine, not just for $H_0$.

lines.text: Reject $H_0$. There is evidence that the mean fill of the machine has changed.

higher.tip: Marks are given for four things: the hypotheses, the calculation, the conclusion and the reason. Write all four.
A conclusion with no calculation behind it earns nothing. Always show the $z$ working.
Put the conclusion in the context of the question. Leaving it out costs a mark.
